tools.name: PowerShell
tools.description:
Executes a given PowerShell command with optional timeout. Working directory persists between commands; shell state (variables, functions) does not.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations via PowerShell: git, npm, docker, and PS cmdlets. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

PowerShell edition: Windows PowerShell 5.1 (powershell.exe)
   - Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `||` are NOT available — they cause a parser error. To run B only if A succeeds: `A; if ($?) { B }`. To chain unconditionally: `A; B`.
   - Ternary (`?:`), null-coalescing (`??`), and null-conditional (`?.`) operators are NOT available. Use `if/else` and explicit `$null -eq` checks instead.
   - Avoid `2>&1` on native executables. In 5.1, redirecting a native command's stderr inside PowerShell wraps each line in an ErrorRecord (NativeCommandError) and sets `$?` to `$false` even when the exe returned exit code 0. stderr is already captured for you — don't redirect it.
   - `>`, `>>`, and `Out-File` usually default to UTF-8 (with BOM) in this environment, but `Set-Content`/`Add-Content` still default to the system ANSI codepage — when writing a file other tools will read, pass `-Encoding utf8` explicitly to `Out-File`/`Set-Content`.
   - `ConvertFrom-Json` returns a PSCustomObject, not a hashtable. `-AsHashtable` is not available.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `Get-ChildItem` (or `ls`) to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

PowerShell Syntax Notes:
   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:
   - head / tail → `Get-Content file -TotalCount N` / `-Tail N`; piped: `| Select-Object -First N` / `-Last N`
   - which → `(Get-Command name).Source`
   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)
   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)
   - Bash control flow (`if [ -f x ]`, `for x in *`, backtick ``cmd`` substitution) is a parser error — use `if (Test-Path x)`, `foreach ($x in ...)`, `$(cmd)`

Exit-code note: `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` suppresses error OUTPUT but the cmdlet failure still causes this tool to report exit 1. To make a cmdlet failure truly non-fatal, promote it to terminating and swallow it: `try { Cmdlet ... -ErrorAction Stop } catch {}` (without `-ErrorAction Stop`, non-terminating errors skip the `catch` and still exit 1).

Interactive and blocking commands (this tool runs with -NonInteractive and stdin attached to the null device — console prompts read EOF or error immediately; GUI prompts can still block until timeout):
   - NEVER use `Read-Host`, `Get-Credential`, `Out-GridView`, `$Host.UI.PromptForChoice`, or `pause`
   - Destructive cmdlets (`Remove-Item`, `Stop-Process`, `Clear-Content`, etc.) may prompt for confirmation. Add `-Confirm:$false` when you intend the action to proceed. Use `-Force` for read-only/hidden items.
   - Never use `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`, or other commands that open an interactive editor

Passing multiline strings (commit messages, file content) to native executables:
   - Use a single-quoted here-string so PowerShell does not expand `$` or backticks inside. The closing `'@` MUST be at column 0 (no leading whitespace) on its own line — indenting it is a parse error:
<example>
git commit -m @'
Commit message here.
Second line with $literal dollar signs.
'@
</example>
   - Use `@'...'@` (single-quoted, literal) not `@"..."@` (double-quoted, interpolated) unless you need variable expansion
   - For arguments containing `-`, `@`, or other characters PowerShell parses as operators, use the stop-parsing token: `git log --% --format=%H`

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes for a foreground command). If not specified, commands will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
  - It is very helpful if you write a clear, concise description of what this command does.
  - If the output exceeds 30000 characters, output will be truncated before being returned to you.
  - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes.
  - Avoid using PowerShell to run commands that have dedicated tools, unless explicitly instructed:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT Get-ChildItem -Recurse)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT Select-String)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT Get-Content)
    - Edit files: Use Edit
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT Set-Content/Out-File)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT Write-Output/Write-Host)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple PowerShell tool calls in a single message.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, chain them in a single PowerShell call (see edition-specific chaining syntax above).
    - Use `;` only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail.
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings and here-strings)
  - Do NOT prefix commands with `cd` or `Set-Location` -- the working directory is already set to the correct project directory automatically.
  - Avoid unnecessary `Start-Sleep` commands:
    - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
    - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — simply run your command using `run_in_background`. There is no need to sleep in this case.
    - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause or consider an alternative approach.
    - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
    - If you must poll an external process, use a check command rather than sleeping first.
    - If you must sleep, keep the duration short to avoid blocking the user.
  - For git commands:
    - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
    - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
    - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

content.content:
1	# NetCortex — Claude Code context (Workstream A, Aun)
2	
3	## Read first
4	
5	- **`docs/PARTNER_PLAN.md`** holds the full project context. Read it before any task. Key sections:
6	  - §2 hackathon rules and partner prizes
7	  - §3 product
8	  - §4 end-to-end flow
9	  - §5 machines and networking
10	  - §6 who builds what
11	  - §7 stack, repo layout, conventions
12	  - §8 shared contracts
13	  - §10 datasets
14	  - §11 timeline and gates
15	  - §13 risks and cut order
16	- **§9 of that doc is the partner's task list (Workstream B).** Do not build those parts.
17	- **This file covers Aun's tasks (Workstream A) and the current state of the machines.**
18	  - If this file and the plan disagree about Workstream A, this file wins.
19	  - Once `packages/core` is merged, the code is the source of truth for contracts.
20	
21	**Deadline:** publish the DEV post by **Mon 19 Oct 2026, 10:00 AM Pakistan time** (hard deadline 11:59 AM PKT). Prefer working and simple over complete and clever.
22	
23	## Current state (keep this section updated)
24	
25	| Machine | Role | Status |
26	|---|---|---|
27	| Laptop (this machine): i7 10th gen, 32 GB RAM, Quadro P520 4 GB | Integration host. All code runs here: Docker, Temporal, CHR, API, workers, collector. | Active. Claude Code in VS Code. |
28	| Mac mini M4, 16 GB (office machine) | **Model server only.** Ollama with `gemma4:e4b` (agent) and `embeddinggemma` (embeddings). `OLLAMA_HOST=0.0.0.0`, `OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE=24h`. **No git, no repo, no code runs there.** | `gemma4:e4b` downloading (about 3 h). Until it's ready, build the agent with Pydantic AI `TestModel`. |
29	| Partner PC: GTX 1660 6 GB, 16 GB RAM, remote | Workstream B via Codex. Runs his own local Ollama for embeddings, plus Gemma 4 E2B/E4B for development. | Working from `docs/PARTNER_PLAN.md`, against the draft contracts. **Needs `packages/core` merged ASAP.** |
30	
31	- **Networking:** Tailscale joins the laptop and Mac (Aun's tailnet). The Mac is shared with the partner.
32	- **Fallback:** if Tailscale fails, pull the partner's code from GitHub and run everything on the laptop. The laptop reaches the Mac over the home LAN.
33	- **Database:** Tiger Cloud (TimescaleDB + pgvector), shared by both people.
34	
35	**Do not download large files on the laptop while the Mac model download runs.** Both share the home connection. Small Docker images and the CHR image are fine.
36	
37	## Folder ownership
38	
39	**Workstream A (edit freely):**
40	- `packages/core`, `packages/agent`, `packages/fixes`
41	- `services/api`, `services/worker`, `services/collector`
42	- `templates/routeros`
43	- `infra/` (except `infra/render`)
44	- `CLAUDE.md`
45	
46	**Workstream B (do not edit; call their interfaces):**
47	- `apps/web`
48	- `packages/detector`, `packages/runbook`, `packages/notify`, `packages/simgen`
49	- `data/`, `eval/`, `experiments/`
50	- `.github/workflows`, `infra/render`, `AGENTS.md`
51	
52	If a partner module is not merged yet, put a stub with the **same interface** in `packages/agent/stubs.py` and switch it out when theirs lands. Never fix a bug in their folders. Write it up for the partner instead.
53	
54	## Tasks, in order
55	
56	### A0. Setup (15 min)
57	
58	- `uv` workspace at the repo root, Python 3.12.
59	- `ruff` and `pytest` configured.
60	- `.gitignore`: `.env`, `data/raw`, `data/generated`, `var/`, `.venv`, `node_modules`.
61	- MIT `LICENSE` if missing.
62	- Install Entire: `entire enable --agent claude-code`, before the first commit.
63	
64	### A1. Contracts: `packages/core` (MOST URGENT, the partner is blocked)
65	
66	1. **`schemas.py`** (pydantic v2): `Cause` and `TemplateId` enums (exact strings from plan §8), `MetricsWindow`, `SeriesForecast`, `DetectionResult`, `RunbookChunk`, `NewsItem`, `NewsCheck`, `ScenarioLabel`, `IncidentReport`, `FixPlan`, `IncidentStatus`.
67	2. **`settings.py`**: one `Settings` class (pydantic-settings) for every env var in plan §8. Add:
68	   - `APPLY_TARGET` (`chr` by default; `real` must be set explicitly)
69	   - `SITE_ID_LIVE` (default `home-lab`)
70	3. **`interfaces.py`**: `Protocol`s for `detect`, `search_runbook`, `speak`, `check_news`, `inject`, `investigate`, with signatures exactly as in plan §8.
71	4. **`db.py`**: psycopg 3 connection pool and small helpers to insert metrics and incidents.
72	5. **`migrations/001_init.sql`**:
73	   - Enable the extensions `timescaledb` and `vector`.
74	   - Create all tables from plan §8.
75	   - Make `probe_metrics`, `iface_metrics` and `forecasts` hypertables.
76	   - Add indexes on `(site_id, time DESC)`.
77	6. **Additions beyond the plan** (Aun owns contracts, so add them now and tell the partner):
78	   - Table `incident_audio(incident_id uuid, lang text, mp3 bytea, created_at timestamptz)` for voice alerts.
79	   - Table `events(id bigserial, time, kind text, payload jsonb)`, plus a `NOTIFY netcortex_events` trigger. The API's SSE stream reads from it.
80	   - Seed a `home-lab` site for the live collector.
81	7. **`.env.example`** with every variable, and these values filled in:
82	   - `AGENT_MODEL=gemma4:e4b`
83	   - `EMBED_MODEL=embeddinggemma`
84	   - `OLLAMA_BASE_URL=http://<mac-tailscale-name>:11434`
85	
86	**Done when:**
87	- `uv run pytest packages/core` passes.
88	- The migration applies cleanly to Tiger Cloud.
89	- The code is merged to `main`.
90	- A short message to the partner lists the merged interfaces and the additions in step 6.
91	
92	### A2. Infra
93	
94	- **`infra/docker-compose.yml`:**
95	  - Temporal dev server (or document `temporal server start-dev` if the CLI is simpler).
96	  - Optional local TimescaleDB with pgvector for offline work.
97	- **`infra/scripts/check_ollama.py`:** confirms the Mac is reachable, both models are listed, and an embedding has 768 dimensions.
98	
99	**Done when:** Temporal UI opens on the laptop and `check_ollama.py` passes. Until the model finishes downloading, it is allowed to report "agent model missing".
100	
101	### A3. Live collector: `services/collector`
102	
103	- An async loop using `icmplib`.
104	- **Pings, every 10 s, for each target:**
105	  - Targets: gateway (home router), upstream hop (find it with a traceroute at startup, then fix it), `1.1.1.1`, `8.8.8.8`, one regional game server (configurable).
106	  - Send a burst of 5 pings per target.
107	  - Latency = average RTT; jitter = standard deviation of the RTTs; loss = % of pings lost.
108	- **Router stats, every 30 s:** read interface and queue stats from the RouterOS REST API (CHR now, a real MikroTik if one is available). If no router is configured, collect pings only.
109	- Writes rows with `source = live` and `site_id = SITE_ID_LIVE`.
110	- Survives errors: log, skip the round, keep running.
111	- One command starts it: `uv run collector`.
112	
113	**Done when:** it runs unattended for an hour and rows keep appearing. **Start it as early as possible.** The partner's calibration needs hours of real data.
114	
115	### A4. Virtual router: `infra/chr`
116	
117	- **`start.sh`:**
118	  - Downloads the CHR x86 image (free license, 1 Mbps cap is fine).
119	  - Boots it in QEMU and forwards the REST API (HTTP) and SSH ports to localhost.
120	  - Waits until the REST API answers.
121	- **`reset.sh`:** restores a clean snapshot.
122	- **`baseline.rsc`:** baseline config:
123	  - `ether1` = primary uplink, `ether2` = backup uplink, `ether3` = LAN
124	  - A couple of simple queues
125	  - A DNS config
126	- **`test_templates.py`:** for every template, applies it with valid sample params, checks the result with `/export`, rolls back, and checks the config matches baseline. Exits non-zero on failure. **The partner's GitHub Actions workflow runs this script.**
127	
128	### A5. Fix templates: `templates/routeros/*.yaml`
129	
130	Four files: `queue_limit`, `failover_route`, `priority_queue`, `dns_servers`. Each has:
131	- `id`
132	- `description` (one plain sentence)
133	- `allowed_causes`
134	- `params` (each with a type plus range, regex or enum)
135	- `apply` (Jinja template of RouterOS commands)
136	- `rollback` (Jinja template)
137	- `verify` (which series should improve, and by how much)
138	
139	`none` is a built-in with no commands.
140	
141	Check every command against RouterOS v7 syntax. If unsure, test it on CHR before committing.
142	
143	### A6. Fix checker: `packages/fixes`
144	
145	1. `validate(template_id, params)`: rejects any value outside the schema.
146	2. `render(template_id, params)`: returns `(commands, rollback)`.
147	3. `dry_run(template_id, params)`, on CHR:
148	   - export the config before
149	   - apply
150	   - export the config after and diff it
151	   - roll back
152	   - export again and confirm it matches the original
153	4. Store the result in `fix_plans`.
154	5. `apply(...)`: used after human approval. It targets CHR unless `APPLY_TARGET=real`.
155	
156	Talk to CHR through the REST API; SSH (`asyncssh`) is the fallback if a command can't run via REST. **Never touch a real router unless `APPLY_TARGET=real` is set explicitly.**
157	
158	### A7. Agent: `packages/agent`
159	
160	- **Model:** a Pydantic AI `Agent` using an OpenAI-compatible provider at `OLLAMA_BASE_URL/v1`, model `AGENT_MODEL`. Output type: `IncidentReport`.

46	## 3. The product: NetCortex
47	
48	NetCortex watches a small network, warns before customers start complaining, explains what is wrong in plain words, and proposes a tested router fix that a human approves.
49	
50	**Who pays and why.** Small neighbourhood internet providers (WISPs), gaming cafes and freelance network engineers. When latency spikes or a link fails, usually in the evening, they get flooded with complaints and lose customers. They don't have a network operations team. NetCortex gives them one for the price of a small box.
51	
52	**What it does, in order:**
53	
54	1. Collects ping results and router interface stats around the clock.
55	2. Forecasts what "normal" should look like for the next few minutes and flags when reality drifts badly away from it.
56	3. Investigates: is the uplink full, is one user hogging it, is the upstream ISP having a bad day, or is one game server's route broken?
57	4. Proposes one fix from a set of tested MikroTik RouterOS templates, with the exact commands and the commands to undo them.
58	5. Tests that fix on a virtual MikroTik router before any human sees it.
59	6. Alerts the owner (dashboard, plus a short voice note in Urdu or English) and waits for Approve or Reject.
60	7. After an approved fix, watches the metrics and rolls back automatically if things did not improve.
61	
62	**Why open models matter here** (this is a required part of the post):
63	
64	- **Privacy:** router configs, network layout and subscriber traffic never leave the premises when the on-site version runs with local models.
65	- **Works when the internet doesn't:** the tool that diagnoses a broken uplink can't depend on that uplink. Gemma runs locally.
66	- **Cost:** no per-token bills, so a small ISP can afford it.
67	- **Control:** we can swap models, fine-tune for RouterOS, and constrain the agent's output.
68	
69	**Honest limits to state in the post:** TabPFN-3.5's cloud API sends anonymised metrics out, and its free license is non-commercial (a paid product would need a commercial license). Cloud add-ons (ElevenLabs, SerpApi, TabPFN cloud) are optional switches. The hosted demo uses replayed and simulated data.
70	
71	**Vendor scope:** MikroTik RouterOS only. It is common among small ISPs and has a free virtual router image (CHR) we can test on. Cisco is out of scope.
72	
73	## 4. System overview and end-to-end flow
74	
75	Data flows from the network into one shared database. Temporal runs detection, the agent and the fix check. The owner approves the fix in the web UI.
76	
77	[embedded content: NetCortex architecture · who builds each part\]
78	
79	The highlighted boxes are the partner's. Every partner box is a plain function or CLI that Aun's workflows call.
80	
81	### The flow, step by step
82	
83	1. **Data in.** The live collector (`source = live`) or the simulator (`source = sim`, via generate, replay or inject) writes rows to `probe_metrics` and `iface_metrics`.
84	2. **Watch.** Every minute, `MonitorSiteWorkflow` calls the partner's `detect()` with the last 30 minutes plus recent history. Forecasts are written to `forecasts`.
85	3. **Open.** If `is_anomaly` is true and no incident is open for that site and cause, an `incidents` row is created and `IncidentWorkflow` starts.
86	4. **Investigate.** Aun's agent runs `investigate()`. It reads the detection result and calls tools: metrics lookup, the partner's `search_runbook()` and `check_news()`, and the template list. It returns an `IncidentReport`.
87	5. **Check the fix.** The fix checker validates the template values, fills the template, applies it on the virtual MikroTik router, reads back the config, then rolls it back. The result goes in `fix_plans`.
88	6. **Alert.** The partner's `speak()` makes a short voice note. The API pushes `incident.opened` and `fix.tested` events to the UI.
89	7. **Decide.** The owner opens the incident in the UI and presses Approve or Reject. The API sends a Temporal signal. The workflow waits up to 2 hours.
90	8. **Apply and verify.** If approved, the fix is applied (to the virtual router in the demo). The workflow watches the key metric for 5 minutes. Improved → `resolved`. Not improved → automatic rollback → `rolled_back`.
91	9. **Trace and score.** Sentry traces every step. The partner's eval runner replays the same path offline to measure accuracy.
92

95	- **On-site product:** one Docker Compose file with self-hosted TimescaleDB, Temporal, the API, the UI and Ollama on a small box at the ISP. Works offline; cloud add-ons are optional switches.
96	- **Hosted demo:** Render + the .tech domain + Tiger Cloud, with replayed simulator data and saved agent reports, clearly labelled.

341	## 9. Partner tasks in detail
342	
343	Do them in this order. Each task lists what it needs, what to build and when it counts as done.
344	
345	### B1. Setup (first hour, during the contracts call)
346	
347	- [ ] Install Tailscale and join Aun's tailnet. Check `curl http://<mac>:11434/api/tags` works.
348	- [ ] Install Entire and run `entire enable --agent codex` in the repo **before the first commit**.
349	- [ ] Install `uv`, Node LTS, Docker. Clone the repo.
350	- [ ] Get API keys: Prior Labs (accept the free non-commercial license at platform.priorlabs.ai), ElevenLabs, SerpApi. Claim the .tech domain and Render credits at hacktoberfest.com/my/promos.
351	- [ ] Install Ollama locally and pull EmbeddingGemma (same tag as Aun). Optional: install local `tabpfn` with CUDA and run its quick-start on the GTX 1660.
352	- [ ] Create `AGENTS.md` for Codex: point it to `docs/PARTNER_PLAN.md`, the folder ownership in section 7, and the rules in section 12.
353	
354	**Done when:** Partner can reach Aun's Ollama and the shared database, and all keys are in a local `.env`.
355	
356	### B2. Datasets and simulator
357	
358	Full detail is in section 10. Summary:
359	
360	- [ ] `simgen ripe` downloads RIPE Atlas ping results for probes in Pakistan → `source = ripe`.
361	- [ ] `simgen calibrate` computes baseline latency, jitter and loss per target type from RIPE data and Aun's live collector rows → `data/calibration.json`.
362	- [ ] `data/sites.yaml` and `data/scenarios.yaml` (scenario catalog).
363	- [ ] `simgen generate --days 7 --seed 42` → Parquet + `scenario_labels`.
364	- [ ] `simgen replay --speed 60` streams generated data into the database as if live.
365	- [ ] `simgen inject` (CLI and the `inject()` function the API calls).
366	- [ ] Eval set in `eval/cases/`.
367	
368	**Done when:** Aun can run `simgen inject --site north-tower --type uplink_congestion` and see rows land in the database within seconds.
369	
370	### B3. Detector (TabPFN)
371	
372	Three jobs inside one `detect()`:
373	
374	1. **Forecast.** For each key series (latency and loss per target, uplink utilisation), predict the next 1–5 minutes with p10/p50/p90 bands. Approach: build lag features (last N values, rolling mean and std, time-of-day, day-of-week, current utilisation) and use TabPFN regression with quantile output, or the TabPFN time-series package if it fits better. Check the Prior Labs docs and pick one.
375	2. **Anomaly score.** Use TabPFN's unsupervised anomaly detection (`tabpfn-extensions`) on a snapshot vector (utilisation, drops, errors, latency and loss across targets). Normalise to 0..1.
376	3. **Cause guess.** Train a TabPFN classifier on feature vectors from labelled simulator windows (`scenario_labels`). Output one of the cause strings plus confidence.
377	
378	**Anomaly rule (tunable):** `is_anomaly` when a key series stays above its p90 for 3 points in a row **or** the anomaly score passes a threshold picked on the eval set.
379	
380	**Practical rules:**
381	
382	- Keep training context small (a few thousand rows). Cache fitted context per site.
383	- `TABPFN_MODE=cloud` uses `tabpfn-client` (TabPFN-3.5). `TABPFN_MODE=local` uses the local package on the GTX 1660. Same interface either way.
384	- Write each forecast to the `forecasts` table so the UI can draw bands.
385	- Fill `evidence` with short plain sentences ("uplink ether1 at 97% for 6 min").
386	- Report precision, recall and detection delay on the eval set in `eval/results/detector.md`.
387	
388	**Done when:** `detect()` flags all injected incidents in a 7-day simulated run with few false alarms, and runs in under 5 seconds per site per call.
389	
390	### B4. Docs search
391	
392	- [ ] Download a small set of official MikroTik RouterOS help pages: queues (simple and queue tree), mangle, routing failover / `check-gateway`, DNS, interface monitoring. Respect the site's terms and robots rules. Save the source URL.
393	- [ ] Split into chunks of about 300–500 words, keeping section titles.
394	- [ ] Embed with EmbeddingGemma through Ollama. Store in `runbook_chunks` with `embed_model`.
395	- [ ] `search_runbook()`: vector search, plus keyword search if time allows (hybrid). Return top `k`.
396	
397	**Done when:** queries like "limit bandwidth for one IP" and "failover default route" return the right page in the top 3.
398	
399	### B5. Side modules
400	
401	- [ ] `speak(text, lang)`: ElevenLabs text-to-speech, a multilingual model that supports Urdu. Return MP3 bytes. Keep text under \~40 words.
402	- [ ] `check_news(provider, target)`: SerpApi search for recent outage reports about the upstream provider or a game server, past 24 hours. Return a short summary and links.
403	- [ ] Both have a mock mode and a timeout. Failing services must never block an incident.
404	
405	**Done when:** both work from a script, and both return safely when keys are missing.
406	
407	### B6. Web UI
408	
409	Build in mock mode first (`NEXT_PUBLIC_API_MODE=mock`, fixtures that follow the API in section 8). Switch to live once Aun's API is up. Mobile-first, dark mode included, Pakistan time on screen.
410	
411	| Page | What it shows | Actions |
412	| --- | --- | --- |
413	| Overview | One card per site: health, uplink usage, worst latency now; a live chart of latency with the forecast band | Open a site or incident |
414	| Incident detail | Timeline; evidence charts; agent summary, cause and confidence; upstream news result; fix commands and rollback commands; CHR test result; voice alert player | Approve, Reject (with confirm) |
415	| Incidents | List, newest first, filter by status and site | Open |
416	| Demo panel | Scenario picker, site picker, duration | Inject scenario |
417	| Settings | Targets per site; switches for TabPFN cloud/local, ElevenLabs, SerpApi | Save |
418	
419	- Live updates through the SSE `/stream`.
420	- Show the fix commands in a monospace block with a copy button. Never imply they were applied before approval.
421	- Add `@sentry/nextjs`.
422	
423	**Done when:** the full approve flow works on a phone screen against the live API.
424	
425	### B7. Hosted demo
426	
427	- [ ] Point the .tech domain at Render.
428	- [ ] Render web service for the UI; Render web service for the API in `DEMO_MODE=true`.
429	- [ ] In demo mode, the API replays simulator data and serves saved agent reports from real runs (Render has no GPU for Gemma). Label this clearly on the page: "Demo: replayed data."
430	- [ ] Optional: during judging, point demo mode at Aun's Mac through a Tailscale Funnel or similar for live agent runs. Only if it's stable.
431	
432	**Done when:** a stranger can open the .tech link and walk through an incident end to end.
433	
434	### B8. CI and GitHub
435	
436	- [ ] Workflow `ci.yml`: `ruff`, `pytest` for Python; lint, type-check and build for `apps/web`.
437	- [ ] Workflow `chr-templates.yml`: boot the CHR x86 image in QEMU on the runner, wait for the REST API, run Aun's `infra/chr/test_templates.py` against every template. The free CHR license (1 Mbps) is enough.
438	- [ ] Enable Copilot code review on PRs.
439	
440	**Done when:** both workflows pass on `main`.
441	
442	### B9. Eval runner
443	
444	- [ ] `eval/run.py` loads each case, rebuilds its metrics window, calls `detect()` and then Aun's `investigate()` function.
445	- [ ] Scores: cause accuracy, template accuracy, valid params rate, CHR dry-run pass rate, time per case.
446	- [ ] Writes `eval/results/agent.md`. These numbers go in the post.
447	
448	### B10. Tinker (optional, only after B1–B9 are working)
449	
450	Tinker does not list Gemma, so this is a comparison, not a replacement. Fine-tune a small Qwen or Llama model on simulator cases (input: detection + evidence; output: cause + template + params). Compare with Gemma 4 E4B on the held-out eval set. Report accuracy, latency and cost.
451	
452	### B11. Post
453	
454	Draft in `docs/post/` from the +8 hour checkpoint: who pays and why, the data story (real Pakistani baselines + simulated incidents), why open models, the first user, the demo link. Aun writes the architecture, agent and safety sections.
455	
456	## 10. Datasets
457	
458	Use real data wherever a source exists, and seed the rest with a simulator calibrated on that real data. The coding agent (Codex or Claude) writes the **generators and scenario specs**, never the raw numbers: LLM-typed time series look fake and have no real structure.
459	
460	### What we need and where it comes from
461	
462	| Dataset | Columns / content | Real source | Seeded? | Output |
463	| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
464	| Ping results | time, site, target, latency, jitter, loss | Aun's live collector (from Sunday); RIPE Atlas public ping results for probes in Pakistan | Yes, simulator adds incidents | `probe_metrics` |
465	| Interface stats | time, site, interface, rx/tx, usage %, drops, errors | Rarely public at this detail | Yes | `iface_metrics` |
466	| Incident labels | scenario type, start/end, affected objects, expected cause, template, params | None | Yes | `scenario_labels` |
467	| Network layout | sites, uplinks, capacity, subscribers, targets | None | Yes, hand-written | `data/sites.yaml` |
468	| Docs for search | MikroTik RouterOS help pages | Official MikroTik docs | No | `runbook_chunks` |
469	| Eval set | 60–100 held-out cases with expected answers | None | Yes, different seeds | `eval/cases/` |
470	| Customer messages | Example English and Urdu messages per cause | None | Yes, agent-written examples | `data/messages.yaml` |
471	| Tinker training set (optional) | detection + evidence → cause + template + params | None | Yes, from simulator | `experiments/tinker/data/` |
472	
473	Optional extra real source: M-Lab's open speed-test data (BigQuery) includes latency for Pakistani networks. Only use it if RIPE Atlas is not enough.
474	
475	### RIPE Atlas (real baselines)
476	
477	1. Find connected probes in Pakistan through the probes API (`/api/v2/probes/` filtered by country code `PK`). Note their network (ASN) to cover several ISPs.
478	2. Find public built-in ping measurements those probes take part in (for example, pings to root DNS servers). Do not hardcode measurement IDs; look them up through `/api/v2/measurements/`.
479	3. Download results through `/api/v2/measurements/<id>/results/` with `start`, `stop` and `probe_ids`. Results come as JSON; parse the RTT list per result into avg latency, jitter (std of RTTs) and loss (sent vs received).
480	4. Pull 7–14 days. Store as Parquet in `data/raw/ripe/` and load a sample into `probe_metrics` with `source = ripe`.
481	5. Be polite to the API: cache downloads, no tight loops.
482	
483	### Calibration
484	
485	`simgen calibrate` reads RIPE rows and Aun's `source = live` rows and writes `data/calibration.json`: per target type (gateway, upstream hop, public DNS, game server) the typical latency, jitter and loss by hour of day. The simulator starts from these values. This lets the post honestly say: "simulated incidents on top of real Pakistani network baselines."
486	
487	### Network layout (`data/sites.yaml`)
488	
489	3 sites, for example `north-tower`, `market-cafe`, `east-relay`. Each has: 1 primary uplink (capacity in Mbps), 0–1 backup uplink, 1–2 wireless backhaul links, 40–200 subscribers, and 5 ping targets (gateway, upstream hop, 1.1.1.1, 8.8.8.8, one regional game server).
490	
491	### Simulator model
492	
493	Time step: 10 s for pings, 30 s for interface stats.
494	
495	- **Demand per subscriber:** a daily curve with a low overnight, a rise in the afternoon and a peak roughly 20:00–01:00 Pakistan time; a weekend boost; random noise; a few random heavy users.
496	- **Uplink usage** = total demand ÷ capacity.
497	- **Latency** = calibrated base + queueing delay that grows gently with usage and shoots up as usage nears 100% (a curve like `k × u / (1 − u)`, capped).
498	- **Loss** starts once usage passes about 95%; jitter grows with usage.
499	- **Noise:** small random spikes so normal data is not too clean.
500	
501	### Scenario catalog (`data/scenarios.yaml`)
502	
503	| Cause | What the data shows | Expected fix template |
504	| --- | --- | --- |
505	| `uplink_congestion` | Uplink usage above 95% for minutes; latency up on all outside targets; gateway fine | `priority_queue` |
506	| `heavy_user` | One subscriber IP takes a large share of the uplink; others slow down | `queue_limit` (that IP) |
507	| `upstream_degradation` | Gateway and usage normal; all outside targets slow or lossy | `none` (notify, check news) |
508	| `game_route_issue` | Only the game server target is bad | `none` (notify, check news) |
509	| `wireless_interference` | Loss and jitter on one backhaul link; usage normal | `none` (send a technician) |
510	| `uplink_down` | Primary uplink loss 100%; backup present | `failover_route` |
511	| `dns_slow` | DNS target slow; other targets fine | `dns_servers` |
512	
513	Each injected scenario writes one `scenario_labels` row with the expected cause, template and params.
514	
515	### Commands to build
516	
517	```
518	simgen ripe --days 14                 # download RIPE Atlas data
519	simgen calibrate                      # write data/calibration.json
520	simgen generate --days 7 --seed 42    # Parquet + labels in data/generated/
521	simgen load --source sim --last 2d    # load a slice into the database
522	simgen replay --speed 60              # stream generated data as if live
523	simgen inject --site north-tower --type heavy_user --duration 15
524	simgen eval-cases --n 80 --seed 1000  # write eval/cases/
525	```
526	
527	## 11. Timeline and checkpoints
528	
529	Five phases, each ending in a gate both people check together on a short call. Hours count from the start of the contracts call on Sunday.
530	
531	[embedded content: Build timeline, 5 phases and 4 gates for both workstreams\]
532	
533	Highlighted cells are the partner's. A gate is passed only when its line is true on Aun's laptop, not just on one machine.
534	
535	**How to run the gates:**
536	
537	- Each gate is a 10-minute call: demo what works, list what is blocked, re-plan the next phase.
538	- If a gate slips by more than an hour, cut scope using the order in section 13. Don't push the post later.
539	- Merge to `main` before every gate, so the integration host always runs the latest code.
540	
541	## 12. Git workflow and rules for Codex
542	
543	Small PRs, owned folders, and no surprise changes to shared code.
544	
545	**Git:**
546	
547	- `main` is protected. Work on short branches named `b/<task>` (partner) and `a/<task>` (Aun), for example `b/detector-forecast`.
548	- Merge through PRs. Copilot reviews every PR; the other person skims and approves. Aim to merge at least every 2 hours so integration never piles up.
549	- Commit early and often: Entire creates a checkpoint on each commit, and those sessions are linked in the post.
550	- Rebase on `main` before opening a PR.
551	
552	**Rules for the Codex session:**
553	
554	1. Only edit folders owned by Workstream B (section 7). To change anything else, open a PR comment or ask Aun.
555	2. Import shared types from `packages/core`. Never copy or redefine them.
556	3. Every module needs: a mock mode, a timeout on every network call, and tests with `pytest` (no network in unit tests; use recorded fixtures).
557	4. Never commit secrets, `.env`, raw downloads or generated Parquet.
558	5. Pin dependencies through `uv.lock` and `package-lock.json`.
559	6. Use only the cause and template strings from section 8.
560	7. Prefer boring, readable code over clever code. Judges and Aun will read it.
561	8. When something in this plan doesn't work as written (an API changed, a package is missing), choose the closest working option, write it down in the PR, and continue.
562	9. Write a short README for every package you create.
563	10. Keep a running `docs/post/notes.md` of interesting findings and numbers. The post needs them.
564	
565	## 13. Risks, fallbacks and definition of done
566	
567	The project is complete when a stranger can open the demo, inject an incident, read the agent's explanation, see a tested fix, approve it, and read a post that explains why open models made it possible.
568	
569	**Risks and fallbacks:**
570	
571	| Risk | Fallback |
572	| --- | --- |
573	| Tailscale can't connect the two networks | Partner runs Ollama locally (Gemma 4 E2B, or E4B if it fits); integration happens on Aun's laptop only |
574	| TabPFN cloud is slow or rate-limited | Switch to `TABPFN_MODE=local` on the GTX 1660; reduce context rows |
575	| TabPFN forecasting too weak on some series | Keep the forecast for latency and usage; rely more on the anomaly score for loss |
576	| RIPE Atlas data is thin for Pakistan | Use Aun's live data + sensible defaults; mention it in the post |
577	| Gemma picks wrong templates | Narrow the agent: pass the detector's cause guess and only the templates allowed for that cause |
578	| CHR won't boot in GitHub Actions | Keep CHR tests on Aun's laptop; CI runs unit tests only; note it in the README |
579	| Render demo can't run Gemma | Saved reports from real runs, clearly labelled |
580	| Tiger Cloud storage fills up | Load fewer days; keep the rest in Parquet |
581	| Running out of time | Cut in this order: Tinker → Settings page → hybrid search → live agent in hosted demo. Never cut the post. |
582	
583	**Definition of done for Workstream B:**
584	
585	- [ ] RIPE Atlas data downloaded and calibration written
586	- [ ] Simulator generates, replays and injects all 7 scenarios with labels
587	- [ ] `detect()` passes on the eval set, results in `eval/results/detector.md`
588	- [ ] `search_runbook()` returns the right docs for the 4 template topics
589	- [ ] `speak()` and `check_news()` work and fail safely
590	- [ ] Web UI: full approve flow works live on a phone
591	- [ ] Hosted demo live on the .tech domain
592	- [ ] CI green; Copilot review enabled
593	- [ ] Agent eval numbers in `eval/results/agent.md`
594	- [ ] Post sections drafted, first-user story written

# NetCortex — Partner Build Plan

Oct 18, 2026 · @Aun Raza

## 1. How to use this document

This is the build brief for **Workstream B (partner)** of NetCortex. It is written to be pasted into a Codex session, which should turn it into a step-by-step task plan and then build it.

- **Who reads it:** the partner and their Codex session. Aun (Workstream A) builds with Claude Code from the same repo: [github.com/aunraza19/NetCortex](https://github.com/aunraza19/NetCortex).
- **What Codex should do first:** read the whole document, then write a task plan for Workstream B only, in the order of section 9, with the checkpoints in section 11.
- **What Codex must not do:** change the shared contracts in section 8 on its own. They belong to Aun. If a contract is wrong or missing something, stop, write the proposed change in a PR description, and ask Aun.
- **When something is unknown** (an exact model tag, an API field name, a package version): check the official docs, pick the current stable option, and note the choice in the PR. Do not guess silently.
- **Where things in this document stop being true:** once Aun merges `packages/core`, that code is the source of truth for schemas and interfaces. This document is the starting point.

Save a copy of this document in the repo as `docs/PARTNER_PLAN.md` so both agents can read it.

## 2. Hackathon context

We are entering the DEV **Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge, Week 2: "Side Hustle"**. The deadline is **Monday 19 October 2026, 11:59 AM Pakistan time**. Our own target is to publish by **10:00 AM**.

- **The prompt:** build something with open-source AI at its core that someone would actually pay for. The open pieces (open-weight models, open frameworks, local inference) must be what makes the project work.
- **The deadline in other time zones:** the page says 18 October. Week 1 ended at 11:59 PM PDT, so we assume Week 2 does too. That is 11:59 AM Monday in Pakistan. Confirm on the Week 2 contest rules page.
- **What we submit:** a post on DEV using the challenge template (it adds the `#devchallenge` and `#hf26challenge` tags). The post explains what we built, who would pay, a demo, why open innovation matters for it, and ideally our first real user.
- **Judging, in order of weight:** writing quality (weighted most heavily), relevance to the prompt and theme, creativity, technical execution, and use of partner technology (optional).
- **Repo rules to respect:** public repo, an open-source license (MIT), and work created during the challenge week.

**Partner prize categories we target.** Each one must do a real job in the system and be clearly shown in the post.

| Partner | Prize | Its job in NetCortex | Built by |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Prior Labs (TabPFN) | $200 | Forecasting, anomaly scoring, cause guessing | Partner |
| Gemma | $200 | The agent model and the embedding model | Aun (agent), Partner (embeddings index) |
| Render | $200 | Hosts the public demo | Partner |
| Tinker (optional) | $200 | Fine-tune a small fix planner and compare with Gemma | Partner, only if time allows |

## 3. The product: NetCortex

NetCortex watches a small network, warns before customers start complaining, explains what is wrong in plain words, and proposes a tested router fix that a human approves.

**Who pays and why.** Small neighbourhood internet providers (WISPs), gaming cafes and freelance network engineers. When latency spikes or a link fails, usually in the evening, they get flooded with complaints and lose customers. They don't have a network operations team. NetCortex gives them one for the price of a small box.

**What it does, in order:**

1. Collects ping results and router interface stats around the clock.
2. Forecasts what "normal" should look like for the next few minutes and flags when reality drifts badly away from it.
3. Investigates: is the uplink full, is one user hogging it, is the upstream ISP having a bad day, or is one game server's route broken?
4. Proposes one fix from a set of tested MikroTik RouterOS templates, with the exact commands and the commands to undo them.
5. Tests that fix on a virtual MikroTik router before any human sees it.
6. Alerts the owner (dashboard, plus a short voice note in Urdu or English) and waits for Approve or Reject.
7. After an approved fix, watches the metrics and rolls back automatically if things did not improve.

**Why open models matter here** (this is a required part of the post):

- **Privacy:** router configs, network layout and subscriber traffic never leave the premises when the on-site version runs with local models.
- **Works when the internet doesn't:** the tool that diagnoses a broken uplink can't depend on that uplink. Gemma runs locally.
- **Cost:** no per-token bills, so a small ISP can afford it.
- **Control:** we can swap models, fine-tune for RouterOS, and constrain the agent's output.

**Honest limits to state in the post:** TabPFN-3.5's cloud API sends anonymised metrics out, and its free license is non-commercial (a paid product would need a commercial license). Cloud add-ons (ElevenLabs, SerpApi, TabPFN cloud) are optional switches. The hosted demo uses replayed and simulated data.

**Vendor scope:** MikroTik RouterOS only. It is common among small ISPs and has a free virtual router image (CHR) we can test on. Cisco is out of scope.

## 4. System overview and end-to-end flow

Data flows from the network into one shared database. Temporal runs detection, the agent and the fix check. The owner approves the fix in the web UI.

[embedded content: NetCortex architecture · who builds each part\]

The highlighted boxes are the partner's. Every partner box is a plain function or CLI that Aun's workflows call.

### The flow, step by step

1. **Data in.** The live collector (`source = live`) or the simulator (`source = sim`, via generate, replay or inject) writes rows to `probe_metrics` and `iface_metrics`.
2. **Watch.** Every minute, `MonitorSiteWorkflow` calls the partner's `detect()` with the last 30 minutes plus recent history. Forecasts are written to `forecasts`.
3. **Open.** If `is_anomaly` is true and no incident is open for that site and cause, an `incidents` row is created and `IncidentWorkflow` starts.
4. **Investigate.** Aun's agent runs `investigate()`. It reads the detection result and calls tools: metrics lookup, the partner's `search_runbook()` and `check_news()`, and the template list. It returns an `IncidentReport`.
5. **Check the fix.** The fix checker validates the template values, fills the template, applies it on the virtual MikroTik router, reads back the config, then rolls it back. The result goes in `fix_plans`.
6. **Alert.** The partner's `speak()` makes a short voice note. The API pushes `incident.opened` and `fix.tested` events to the UI.
7. **Decide.** The owner opens the incident in the UI and presses Approve or Reject. The API sends a Temporal signal. The workflow waits up to 2 hours.
8. **Apply and verify.** If approved, the fix is applied (to the virtual router in the demo). The workflow watches the key metric for 5 minutes. Improved → `resolved`. Not improved → automatic rollback → `rolled_back`.
9. **Trace and score.** Sentry traces every step. The partner's eval runner replays the same path offline to measure accuracy.

### Two ways it runs

- **On-site product:** one Docker Compose file with self-hosted TimescaleDB, Temporal, the API, the UI and Ollama on a small box at the ISP. Works offline; cloud add-ons are optional switches.
- **Hosted demo:** Render + the .tech domain + Tiger Cloud, with replayed simulator data and saved agent reports, clearly labelled.

### Cause and template vocabulary

These strings are used by the simulator, detector, agent, eval and UI. Do not invent others.

- **Causes:** `uplink_congestion`, `heavy_user`, `upstream_degradation`, `game_route_issue`, `wireless_interference`, `uplink_down`, `dns_slow`, `normal`.
- **Fix templates:** `queue_limit` (limit one IP or subnet), `failover_route` (backup default route with `check-gateway=ping`), `priority_queue` (prioritise gaming and DNS traffic), `dns_servers` (switch DNS resolvers), `none` (no config fix; notify only).

Three jobs inside one `detect()`:

1. **Forecast.** For each key series (latency and loss per target, uplink utilisation), predict the next 1–5 minutes with p10/p50/p90 bands. Approach: build lag features (last N values, rolling mean and std, time-of-day, day-of-week, current utilisation) and use TabPFN regression with quantile output, or the TabPFN time-series package if it fits better. Check the Prior Labs docs and pick one.
2. **Anomaly score.** Use TabPFN's unsupervised anomaly detection (`tabpfn-extensions`) on a snapshot vector (utilisation, drops, errors, latency and loss across targets). Normalise to 0..1.
3. **Cause guess.** Train a TabPFN classifier on feature vectors from labelled simulator windows (`scenario_labels`). Output one of the cause strings plus confidence.

**Anomaly rule (tunable):** `is_anomaly` when a key series stays above its p90 for 3 points in a row **or** the anomaly score passes a threshold picked on the eval set.

**Practical rules:**

- Keep training context small (a few thousand rows). Cache fitted context per site.
- `TABPFN_MODE=cloud` uses `tabpfn-client` (TabPFN-3.5). `TABPFN_MODE=local` uses the local package on the GTX 1660. Same interface either way.
- Write each forecast to the `forecasts` table so the UI can draw bands.
- Fill `evidence` with short plain sentences ("uplink ether1 at 97% for 6 min").
- Report precision, recall and detection delay on the eval set in `eval/results/detector.md`.

**Done when:** `detect()` flags all injected incidents in a 7-day simulated run with few false alarms, and runs in under 5 seconds per site per call.

## 10. Datasets

Use real data wherever a source exists, and seed the rest with a simulator calibrated on that real data. The coding agent (Codex or Claude) writes the **generators and scenario specs**, never the raw numbers: LLM-typed time series look fake and have no real structure.

### What we need and where it comes from

| Dataset | Columns / content | Real source | Seeded? | Output |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Ping results | time, site, target, latency, jitter, loss | Aun's live collector (from Sunday); RIPE Atlas public ping results for probes in Pakistan | Yes, simulator adds incidents | `probe_metrics` |
| Interface stats | time, site, interface, rx/tx, usage %, drops, errors | Rarely public at this detail | Yes | `iface_metrics` |
| Incident labels | scenario type, start/end, affected objects, expected cause, template, params | None | Yes | `scenario_labels` |
| Network layout | sites, uplinks, capacity, subscribers, targets | None | Yes, hand-written | `data/sites.yaml` |

| Eval set | 60–100 held-out cases with expected answers | None | Yes, different seeds | `eval/cases/` |
| Customer messages | Example English and Urdu messages per cause | None | Yes, agent-written examples | `data/messages.yaml` |

Optional extra real source: M-Lab's open speed-test data (BigQuery) includes latency for Pakistani networks. Only use it if RIPE Atlas is not enough.

### RIPE Atlas (real baselines)

1. Find connected probes in Pakistan through the probes API (`/api/v2/probes/` filtered by country code `PK`). Note their network (ASN) to cover several ISPs.
2. Find public built-in ping measurements those probes take part in (for example, pings to root DNS servers). Do not hardcode measurement IDs; look them up through `/api/v2/measurements/`.
3. Download results through `/api/v2/measurements/<id>/results/` with `start`, `stop` and `probe_ids`. Results come as JSON; parse the RTT list per result into avg latency, jitter (std of RTTs) and loss (sent vs received).
4. Pull 7–14 days. Store as Parquet in `data/raw/ripe/` and load a sample into `probe_metrics` with `source = ripe`.
5. Be polite to the API: cache downloads, no tight loops.

### Calibration

`simgen calibrate` reads RIPE rows and Aun's `source = live` rows and writes `data/calibration.json`: per target type (gateway, upstream hop, public DNS, game server) the typical latency, jitter and loss by hour of day. The simulator starts from these values. This lets the post honestly say: "simulated incidents on top of real Pakistani network baselines."

### Network layout (`data/sites.yaml`)

3 sites, for example `north-tower`, `market-cafe`, `east-relay`. Each has: 1 primary uplink (capacity in Mbps), 0–1 backup uplink, 1–2 wireless backhaul links, 40–200 subscribers, and 5 ping targets (gateway, upstream hop, 1.1.1.1, 8.8.8.8, one regional game server).

### Simulator model

Time step: 10 s for pings, 30 s for interface stats.

- **Demand per subscriber:** a daily curve with a low overnight, a rise in the afternoon and a peak roughly 20:00–01:00 Pakistan time; a weekend boost; random noise; a few random heavy users.
- **Uplink usage** = total demand ÷ capacity.
- **Latency** = calibrated base + queueing delay that grows gently with usage and shoots up as usage nears 100% (a curve like `k × u / (1 − u)`, capped).
- **Loss** starts once usage passes about 95%; jitter grows with usage.
- **Noise:** small random spikes so normal data is not too clean.

### Scenario catalog (`data/scenarios.yaml`)

| Cause | What the data shows | Expected fix template |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `uplink_congestion` | Uplink usage above 95% for minutes; latency up on all outside targets; gateway fine | `priority_queue` |
| `heavy_user` | One subscriber IP takes a large share of the uplink; others slow down | `queue_limit` (that IP) |
| `upstream_degradation` | Gateway and usage normal; all outside targets slow or lossy | `none` (notify, check news) |
| `game_route_issue` | Only the game server target is bad | `none` (notify, check news) |
| `wireless_interference` | Loss and jitter on one backhaul link; usage normal | `none` (send a technician) |
| `uplink_down` | Primary uplink loss 100%; backup present | `failover_route` |
| `dns_slow` | DNS target slow; other targets fine | `dns_servers` |

Each injected scenario writes one `scenario_labels` row with the expected cause, template and params.

### Commands to build

```
simgen ripe --days 14                 # download RIPE Atlas data
simgen calibrate                      # write data/calibration.json
simgen generate --days 7 --seed 42    # Parquet + labels in data/generated/
simgen load --source sim --last 2d    # load a slice into the database
simgen replay --speed 60              # stream generated data as if live
simgen inject --site north-tower --type heavy_user --duration 15
simgen eval-cases --n 80 --seed 1000  # write eval/cases/
```

# Contract questions for Aun

These are proposals and integration questions only. They do not change shared contracts. Aun must approve the answers and publish the source-of-truth definitions before Workstream B binds to them.

## Core package and shared types

- Confirm the distribution name and import name for `packages/core`; `netcortex_core` is the expected import namespace, but the distribution name is unresolved.
- Publish supported Python version, package exports, schema versions, and compatibility policy.
- Confirm exact types and field names for probe/interface metrics, forecasts, incidents, detection results, incident reports, fix plans, and template parameters.
- Clarify timestamp timezone/format, units, nullability, source labels, and identifier formats.

## Settings and API

- Confirm Settings field names, defaults, environment variable names, validation behavior, and secret handling.
- Confirm API base path, auth mechanism, owner/user role mapping, and how demo mode is represented.
- Provide request/response examples and explicit status/error payloads for incident list/detail, approval/rejection, history, and health endpoints.
- Define explicit failure semantics for upstream timeouts, unavailable model/provider, stale data, authorization failure, and partial results. Errors must remain distinguishable from a successful empty response.

## SSE and subscriber telemetry

- Confirm SSE endpoint, event envelope, event IDs/replay behavior, heartbeat cadence, reconnect expectations, and event names/payloads (`incident.opened`, `fix.tested`, and others).
- Specify whether subscriber identifiers/IPs are exposed, redacted, or role-gated in API events and the UI; identify retention and access policy.
- Clarify how a subscriber can be identified for heavy-user analysis without exposing unnecessary personal data.
- Extend MetricsWindow/storage with observed per-subscriber traffic and IP identity;
  aggregate interface counters cannot identify an offending user. Supplemental
  simulator fixtures are experimental until this contract is approved.
- Add explicit DNS resolution duration/outcome observations; ICMP RTT to a DNS
  server is not a DNS lookup measurement.
- Publish target roles and interface/backhaul mapping, uplink capacities and
  configured backup gateways so causes and fix parameters derive from observations.
- Define Settings read/update API endpoints before enabling editable UI Settings.

## Timing and role mapping

- Confirm collection intervals, detector lookback/history window, forecast horizon, and freshness thresholds for probe and interface telemetry.
- Confirm role mapping for owner, operator, and read-only/demo viewers, including permissions for approve/reject and subscriber-level evidence.
- Confirm workflow timing and expiry behavior for approvals and for post-change observation/rollback.

## Forecast persistence and injection lifecycle

- Define a unique key and conflict/upsert policy for forecasts, including site, metric/target, model/version, and forecast timestamp dimensions as appropriate.
- Identify the sole forecast writer and the expected transactional behavior when a detection run retries.
- Define simulator injection start/end semantics, source labeling, scenario-label linkage, cleanup/expiry behavior, and whether injections can overlap.
- Clarify how generated/replayed rows differ from injected rows and which records are safe to retain in a hosted demo.

## Router test integration

- Confirm location and invocation contract for Aun's CHR harness, expected CHR image/license setup, and machine-readable result format.
- Workstream B CI will call `infra/chr/test_templates.py` only when Aun provides it. Until then, the router template CI gate is pending; no substitute test will be reported as a router test.

# Contract questions for Aun

These are proposals and integration questions only. They do not change shared contracts. Aun must approve the answers and publish the source-of-truth definitions before Workstream B binds to them.

## Core package and shared types

- Confirm the distribution name and import name for `packages/core`; `netcortex_core` is the expected import namespace, but the distribution name is unresolved.
- Publish supported Python version, package exports, schema versions, and compatibility policy.
- Confirm exact types and field names for probe/interface metrics, forecasts, incidents, detection results, incident reports, fix plans, and template parameters.
- Clarify timestamp timezone/format, units, nullability, source labels, and identifier formats.

## Settings and API

- Confirm Settings field names, defaults, environment variable names, validation behavior, and secret handling.
- Confirm API base path, auth mechanism, owner/user role mapping, and how demo mode is represented.
- Provide request/response examples and explicit status/error payloads for incident list/detail, approval/rejection, history, and health endpoints.
- Define explicit failure semantics for upstream timeouts, unavailable model/provider, stale data, authorization failure, and partial results. Errors must remain distinguishable from a successful empty response.

## SSE and subscriber telemetry

- Confirm SSE endpoint, event envelope, event IDs/replay behavior, heartbeat cadence, reconnect expectations, and event names/payloads (`incident.opened`, `fix.tested`, and others).
- Specify whether subscriber identifiers/IPs are exposed, redacted, or role-gated in API events and the UI; identify retention and access policy.
- Clarify how a subscriber can be identified for heavy-user analysis without exposing unnecessary personal data.
- Extend MetricsWindow/storage with observed per-subscriber traffic and IP identity;
  aggregate interface counters cannot identify an offending user. Supplemental
  simulator fixtures are experimental until this contract is approved.
- Add explicit DNS resolution duration/outcome observations; ICMP RTT to a DNS
  server is not a DNS lookup measurement.
- Publish target roles and interface/backhaul mapping, uplink capacities and
  configured backup gateways so causes and fix parameters derive from observations.
- Define Settings read/update API endpoints before enabling editable UI Settings.

## Timing and role mapping

- Confirm collection intervals, detector lookback/history window, forecast horizon, and freshness thresholds for probe and interface telemetry.
- Confirm role mapping for owner, operator, and read-only/demo viewers, including permissions for approve/reject and subscriber-level evidence.
- Confirm workflow timing and expiry behavior for approvals and for post-change observation/rollback.

## Forecast persistence and injection lifecycle

- Define a unique key and conflict/upsert policy for forecasts, including site, metric/target, model/version, and forecast timestamp dimensions as appropriate.
- Identify the sole forecast writer and the expected transactional behavior when a detection run retries.
- Define simulator injection start/end semantics, source labeling, scenario-label linkage, cleanup/expiry behavior, and whether injections can overlap.
- Clarify how generated/replayed rows differ from injected rows and which records are safe to retain in a hosted demo.

## Router test integration

- Confirm location and invocation contract for Aun's CHR harness, expected CHR image/license setup, and machine-readable result format.
- Workstream B CI will call `infra/chr/test_templates.py` only when Aun provides it. Until then, the router template CI gate is pending; no substitute test will be reported as a router test.
